entries.title: Man charged in Lower West Side fatal stabbing of 86-year-old
entries.summary: <p>A man is facing murder charges in the fatal stabbing of an elderly man in Lower West Side Monday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Alejandro Lozano, 44, is charged with first-degree murder, first-degree attempted murder and an additional murder count with probability of death or great bodily harm, police said.</p><p>Lozano is accused of stabbing an 86-year-old man and a 78-year-old woman, both his upstairs neighbors, during an argument at a residence in the 2100 block of West 19th Street about 8:58 p.m. Monday, according to police.</p><p>The injured woman was taken to Stroger Hospital in fair condition. The wounded 86-year-old died after being taken to Mt. Sinai Hospital.</p><p>Officials said the stabbing was “domestic related.”</p><p>Lozano is scheduled to appear in court Thursday.</p>

entries.title: Luke Glendening follows 'crazy ride' to Blackhawks, who need his faceoff skills
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> are the latest stop on veteran NHL center Luke Glendening's meandering late-career road.</p><p>"I was talking to my wife [about how] in the last 12 months — well, a little bit more — I've been on three PTOs and waivers twice," Glendening said Wednesday. "It's been a crazy ride. Five different cities. But every day in this league is a blessing."</p><p>He played for the Lightning in 2024-25 and for the Devils and Flyers in 2025-26. Then he rejoined the Lightning for training camp in September on a tryout deal but didn't get signed.</p><p>He inked a new PTO with the Rangers on Oct. 19 and parlayed that into a one-year contract, making four appearances for them. Then he wound up on waivers and was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/22/blackhawks-claim-luke-glendening-waivers-rangers-faceoffs" >claimed</a> Sunday by the Hawks, with whom he will debut Wednesday against the Kraken.</p><p>It should help Glendening that Hawks coach Jeff Blashill knows him well, having previously coached him with AHL Grand Rapids, with the Red Wings and with the Lightning. It already helped him get this Hawks gig, for one thing.</p><p>Blashill said Glendening is "good at what he's good at," namely three things: winning faceoffs, killing penalties and eating minutes against tough competition. Blashill noted Flyers coach Rick Tocchet deployed Glendening against the Penguins' top forwards in the playoffs last season.</p><p>"Doesn't mean he's going to check the other team's best every night here," Blashill added, "but certainly [he's] somebody I believe can go out and give us real trustworthy minutes."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe height="578" width="325" src="https://www.tiktok.com/player/v1/7712278236528479501?embed_from=oembed&music_info=1&description=1&autoplay=1&muted=1" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; fullscreen; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" allowfullscreen loading="lazy"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Even at age 37, Glendening is still a fast skater. Combined with his physicality, that makes him effective on the forecheck, which is a point of emphasis for the Hawks.</p><p>Veteran winger Jordan Greenway will make his second consecutive appearance Wednesday after three consecutive healthy scratches, but it'll be interesting to see if Glendening's presence displaces Greenway moving forward. Greenway's lack of speed has made his forechecking inconsistent, and he hasn't been as physical as hoped, either.</p><p>It's worth noting Glendening contributes nothing offensively. He entered Wednesday with 16 points in 151 games since the start of 2024-25. But the Hawks aren't expecting that from him anyway.</p><p>The faceoff dot is the most important area where he can help. The Hawks rank last in the league in faceoff percentage, which isn't too surprising considering how young their centers are. They've direly lacked a reliable guy to send out for high-leverage draws on penalty kills or when protecting late leads.</p><p>Glendening, on the other hand, is one of the best active draw-takers in the league, sporting a 55.7% career faceoff percentage. He has been above 52% for 12 consecutive seasons. </p><p>He explained it was a late-blooming skill, considering he was a winger at the University of Michigan. He didn't get moved to center until an ECHL stint with Toledo in 2012.</p><p>"As I moved up, they were like, 'If you can't start figuring out how to win faceoffs, you're not going to be in this league,'" he said. "I didn't have a lot of other desirable attributes, so they were like, 'If you can figure this out, you can find a niche role.' </p><p>"That's why I tried to do. I studied. I'd take them as often as I can in practice. Some nights, it doesn't go your way, so you've got to keep building. There's been nights I've been terrible, and there's been nights I've been good."</p><p>Perhaps the best possible thing Glendening could do is pass along knowledge about some tricks of the faceoff trade to young cornerstone Hawks like Frank Nazar, Anton Frondell and (eventually) Connor Bedard.</p><p>"I can name someone at every stop...whether that be a coach, another player, a GM [or] a skills coach who have poured into me and helped me a little bit," he said. "If I can pass that along, I would love to."</p>

entries.title: DK Heard's clutch free throws seal King's comeback win against De La Salle
entries.summary: <p>It’s been a tumultuous few months for DK Heard. He was a star freshman at Mount Carmel last season, but had to leave at the start of this school year and transferred to King, which is extremely close to his home.</p><p>There is always drama around a transfer that takes place shortly before the season begins, and perhaps weathering all that helped Heard focus with the game on the line, the crowd roaring, and De La Salle calling multiple timeouts to ice him at the free-throw line on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-basketball/scores/2026/11/25/illinois-high-school-basketball-scores-chicago" >Wednesday</a>.</p><p>Heard had a rough day at the line overall, but he made two free throws when it counted, sinking both with 0.3 seconds left to give the visiting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-basketball-rankings/2026/11/17/michael-obriens-preseason-super-25-illinois-high-school-basketball-rankings" >No. 21 Jaguars</a> a 59-58 win.</p><p>“I had to win the game for my team,” Heard said. “That was it. [The timeouts] didn’t impact me at all. I knew I was going to knock the free throws down.”</p><p>Heard went 3-for-9 from the line before hitting the game-winners.</p><p>“I had no doubt in my mind that DK Heard was going to make those two free throws at the end,” King coach Jerell Parker said. “In fact, he came and told me at the five-minute mark that we were going to win the game, that he was going to come up with something big for me.”</p><p>Heard, a 6-4 guard, finished with 19 points and 10 rebounds. entries.title: Blackhawks sweep road trip with gritty win over Kraken
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — From the moment the NHL schedule was announced in July, it was clear the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' November included both the hardest possible road trip and the easiest possible road trip.</p><p>The hardest trip — against the Panthers, Lightning and Hurricanes — went so badly that it prompted an internal reckoning and a state-of-the-union address by general manager Kyle Davidson.</p><p>It turns out the Hawks just needed the easiest trip to come around. A gritty 3-1 victory over the Kraken on Wednesday completed a three-game Hawks sweep of the Pacific Northwest, following wins over the equally benign <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/21/blackhawks-flames-sam-rinzel-wyatt-kaiser-martin-pospisil" >Flames</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/22/blackhawks-canucks-roman-kantserov-hat-trick" >Canucks</a>.</p><p>In a matter of five days, the Hawks' road record improved from 0-8-1 to 3-8-1.</p><p>"There was a lot of buy-in today," said goalie Spencer Knight, who made 29 saves and barely missed out on his first shutout since January. "A lot of commitment to play a good road game and...sticking with it throughout the game. It was fun for me to see."</p><p>Said forward Anton Frondell: "We always knew that we could be this team that we’ve shown the last three games."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Roman Kantserov with one of the most impressive empty-net goals I’ve seen: <a href="https://t.co/6hc3bAu6F7">pic.twitter.com/6hc3bAu6F7</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2125822976067240288?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 26, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Kraken had the majority of possession and outshot the Hawks 30-19, but the visitors generally kept them to the outside and blocked a number of shots that could've further inflated that margin. They were credited with 19 blocks to the Kraken's seven.</p><p>Even Patrick Kane — an unlikely candidate — made a massive block with his right foot in the final minutes, which forced him to the locker room early. Coach Jeff Blashill wasn't sure of Kane's status afterward.</p><p>"Early in the season, we weren't committed enough [to block shots], and I think we've gotten much better at it," Blashill said. "We're in lanes, and we're way more committed to blocking shots. It's one of those things that's a little bit contagious.</p><p>"It doesn't come without some risk, and I certainly don't want a guy like Patrick to miss time or anything like that. But it is part of the game now, and it's part of the commitment to winning that you have to have."</p><p>The game remained goalless into the third period until Cole Smith tipped in an Ethan Del Mastro shot with 14 minutes left.</p><p>Roman Kantserov then extended his NHL rookie goal-scoring lead with two more goals, including an extremely impressive empty-netter where he stripped Kraken forward Matthew Wood deep inside the Hawks' zone, turned and hit the cage from 154 feet away. He's now on a stunning 47-goal pace this season.</p><p>"Those are paces that are hard to keep up, so we'll see," Blashill said. "But he finds ways to score in different ways. Obviously I trust him enough to have him out there five-on-six, as well. He's a good defensive player."</p>

entries.title: Chicago Public Media audience, staff share what they are grateful for this Thanksgiving
entries.summary: <p>Thanksgiving is often centered on preparing a feast and sharing a meal with family and friends.</p><p>But the holiday also offers an opportunity to pause and reflect on what people are grateful for. While some make a habit of practicing gratitude every day, Thanksgiving serves as a reminder to appreciate the people and things that bring meaning to their lives.</p><p>Chicago Public Media listeners and staff shared what they are thankful for this holiday on WBEZ’s Say More with Mary Dixon & Patrick Smith — joining us for a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/say-more-with-mary-dixon-patrick-smith/2026/11/17/say-more-is-grateful-for-wbez-members" target="_blank" ><u>live show</u></a> in our performance studio and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/say-more-with-mary-dixon-patrick-smith/2026/11/25/say-more-gives-thanks" target="_blank" ><u>calling in</u></a> a day before it’s time to slice the turkey.</p><h3><b>Suzanne Meyering, Rogers Park</b></h3><p>Suzanne Meyering said she was grateful for her women friends and siblings, especially her sister, Eileen.</p><p>Meyering shared that Eileen was the primary caregiver for their mother until she passed at 95 years old.</p><p>“She kept her alive during the pandemic, and she took care of her when she was bedridden, and I couldn't have done it without her,” Meyering said.</p><p>Eileen will soon move to Rogers Park to live close to her sister.</p><h3><b>Nitha Nagubadi, Loop </b></h3><p>Nitha Nagubadi said she was grateful for her parents, who left India for the entries.title: ESPN can't hide from Joe Buck-Troy Aikman feud forever
entries.summary: <p>We’re just over 12 weeks away from the Super Bowl, but it will be the topic of conversation Tuesday, when ESPN hosts media day in New York. One of the subjects figures to be Troy Aikman’s beef with TV partner Joe Buck, which shows no sign of ending.</p><p>Here’s the thing: Neither will be on hand to talk about it.</p><p>According to Sports Business Journal, the keynote speakers will be NFL commissioner Roger Goodell, Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro and ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro. ESPN’s Mike Greenberg will host, but none of the game broadcast talent will be there.</p><p>The network can’t kick the can down the road forever. Eventually, it will run into a wall and have to answer for a feud that already has overshadowed its enormous plans — and one it helped create.</p><p>That was when it offered Buck a new contract but not Aikman, and it chose not to tell the latter. It was a stunning reversal for ESPN, which hired the duo away from Fox to finally solidify its “Monday Night Football” booth, not to mention its relationship with the NFL, which had soured under previous ESPN president John Skipper.</p><p>Now a 25-year relationship has soured, and it’s spilling into public view. Last month, Aikman told a Dallas radio station that he’ll be a free agent after the season. Last week, Aikman told the same station that Buck “always wanted a one-man booth.” What might he say next, and will ESPN do anything about it?</p><p>It must be surreal for Pitaro, who worked tirelessly to get ESPN its first Super Bowl, only to see the run-up to it devolve into this.</p><p>“Are we happy about the media coverage recently? Of course not. It’s been disappointing,” Pitaro said at an SBJ conference last week. “But these guys are professionals, and they’re delivering every week. If you watched it [Nov. 16], another super high-quality production and telecast, and I’d fully expect that to continue through the season and through the Super Bowl.”</p><p>It sounds like ESPN will ride out Aikman’s discontent, even if he stays a malcontent. The network clearly has hitched itself to Buck, who might have endeared himself more to the Disney family than Aikman, appearing on other shows such as “ESPN Jeopardy!” Aikman’s outside interests, such as his beer brand and formerly consulting for the Dolphins, might not show the commitment to the company that bosses want.</p><p>It brings to mind another long ESPN relationship that went sideways: “Mike & Mike in the Morning,” with Greenberg and Golic, which aired on ESPN Radio for 18 years. The network gave Greenberg his own TV show, and Golic was left to fend for himself. He left after 25 years, though he returned this year to co-host a radio show with his son.</p><p>Buck and Aikman form one of the best broadcast tandems of all time, regardless of sport. And Pitaro is right: They have maintained a professional broadcast. But no matter what ESPN’s reasoning is for moving on from Aikman, it didn’t have to end like this. This was a failure of communication on ESPN’s part, but also Buck’s. He could’ve been forthcoming about his situation well before it came to a head Oct. 12 in the SoFi Stadium booth, where the two had their infamous blow-up before the Bills-Rams game.</p><p>It doesn’t make for a happy couple, especially considering the Super Bowl is on Valentine’s Day.</p><h3>Remote patrol</h3><p>WGN TV made a fine choice in hiring <b>Coley Harvey</b> to replace <b>Jarrett Payton</b>, who left to co-host The Score’s morning show. Harvey, a Northwestern alum, has worked for several national outlets, including ESPN, where he shined reporting on Bills safety <b>Damar Hamlin’s</b> on-field cardiac arrest in 2023.</p><p>• TNT is giving Blackhawks fans a treat, putting <b>Eddie Olczyk</b> and <b>Darren Pang</b> on its broadcast of Rangers-Hawks on Friday. Adding to the fun, <b>Paul Bissonnette</b>, who has antagonized the Hawks this season, will be in the studio. Coverage begins at 4 p.m.</p>

entries.title: What to watch for in Bears-Lions game: Ben Johnson vs. Amon-Ra St. Brown
entries.summary: <h3><b>WHEN THE BEARS HAVE THE BALL</b></h3><p>The idea that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/20/bears-coach-ben-johnsons-straight-talk-changes-the-conversation-at-halas-hall" >Ben Johnson</a> was holding back against the Saints on Sunday because he didn’t want to tip his hand to the Lions is farcical, but he might bring a little extra to Ford Field on Thursday.</p><p>Johnson needs all the firepower he can find to tangle with his former team, which swept the Bears last season. The Lions are the No. 5 scoring offense, and falling behind against them is perilous.</p><p>There’s also added motivation going against the Lions, even though Johnson wouldn’t say that. He was steaming after both losses last season, calling out his team’s inadequate practice habits after the first and saying after the second, “I was disappointed with the offense as a whole; I let those guys know that.”</p><p>Both games were duds for the offense against a middling Detroit defense. In the blowout loss at Ford Field in Week 2, the Bears were down 14 by halftime, and in the rematch, they totaled a season-low 270 yards.</p><p>One of the Bears’ next steps is to establish themselves as the bully of the NFC North, which hasn’t happened yet despite winning the division decisively last season. They went 2-4 in the North and are off to an 0-2 start this season.</p><p>Johnson can’t get where he wants to go without toppling his old team. The Lions are hunting for their third division title in four seasons, and the Bears will have to outmuscle them to stay on top.</p><h3><b>WHEN THE LIONS HAVE THE BALL</b></h3><p>When Johnson listed the Lions’ many offensive weapons, it was interesting that he was the one who developed that powerful young core as Detroit’s offensive coordinator. There’s a lot of talent there, but he helped those players reach another level.</p><p>That’s especially true of wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown.</p><p>He was good right away — it’s still hard to believe he was a fourth-round pick in 2021 — but Johnson helped him become great. He’s dangerous lining up anywhere on the field, and the Bears’ cornerbacks have been inconsistent this season. If the Lions’ offensive line is able to buy time against the new and improved Bears’ pass rush, covering St. Brown is going to be a massive challenge for Jaylon Johnson, Tyrique Stevenson and Malik Muhammad.</p><p>Johnson created a monster who averaged 1,250 yards over his first five seasons. With 70 catches, 792 yards and eight touchdowns already, he’s on track for another great one.</p><p>St. Brown has been an absolute nightmare against the Bears, and in two games last season, he totaled 254 yards and three touchdowns on 20 catches.</p><p>When Johnson left the Lions for the Bears after the 2024 season, St. Brown was happy for him, but promised, “Two times a year, Ben, we’re going to [mess] you up.” Johnson replied, as St. Brown recalled, “I’m going to [mess] you up.” They were being playful, but so far it’s St. Brown 2, Johnson 0 when it comes to messing each other up.</p>

entries.title: Musk's big bucks didn't pay off in midterms
entries.summary: <p>Elon Musk, the world's richest man, <a class="Link" href="https://qz.com/elon-musk-474-million-political-donations-midterms-110226" target="_blank" >spent</a> nearly half a billion dollars in a vain attempt to help Republicans win this month's midterm elections. </p><p>"I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it," he <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/video/business/dealbook/100000011295981/elon-musk-spending-midterm-elections.html" target="_blank" >told</a> The New York Times last week.</p><p>Contrary to what advocates of stricter campaign finance regulation often <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2010/11/09/you-are-now-free-to-speak-abou/" target="_blank" >imply</a>, Musk noted that "American elections are not just about money." That point was repeatedly confirmed by midterm races that Republicans lost, sometimes by a lot, despite large spending advantages.</p><p>"Republicans have an enormous financial edge in this year's midterms," Times reporter Shane Goldmacher <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/us/politics/midterms-republican-spending-edge.html" target="_blank" >noted</a> in October. In the seven U.S. Senate races that the Cook Political Report described as toss-ups, Goldmacher reported, "Republicans are outspending Democrats on advertising by $947 million to $625 million" — "a breathtaking advantage of more than $320 million in the key races that could determine which party wins control of the Senate."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-150000" name="module-150000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Democrats <a class="Link" href="https://ballotpedia.org/Election_results%2C_2026%3A_U.S._Senate" target="_blank" >won</a> all those Senate races, plus 15 more. In Texas, for example, James Talarico <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/texas-results/" target="_blank" >beat</a> Ken Paxton by 12 points, even though pro-Paxton spending, including <a class="Link" href="https://www.marketwatch.com/livecoverage/midterm-elections-2026-results-economy-stocks/card/elon-musk-spent-big-to-help-texas-republican-ken-paxton-in-his-senate-run-it-wasn-t-enough--5iPE2B26uob3XPoOK8eT" target="_blank" >$212 million</a> that Musk contributed, <a class="Link" href="https://votelog.org/investigations/texas-senate-general-money" target="_blank" >exceeded</a> pro-Talarico spending by about 35%.</p><p>Money clearly was not enough to make up for the <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/27/ken-paxtons-primary-victory-shows-how-trumps-grudges-undermine-his-partys-interests/" target="_blank" >manifest defects</a> of a <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/10/27/ken-paxton-survived-indictment-impeachment-and-scandal-can-he-survive-a-senate-race/" target="_blank" >scandal-plagued</a> candidate like Paxton, who also suffered from his close association with President Donald Trump. By contrast, that association enabled Paxton to prevail against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, in the Republican primary</p><p>In a contest dominated by the MAGA faithful, <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/27/ken-paxtons-primary-victory-shows-how-trumps-grudges-undermine-his-partys-interests/" target="_blank" >Trump’s favor</a> easily overcame Cornyn's vastly superior financial resources. Although Cornyn and his supporters <a class="Link" href="https://www.houstonchronicle.com/politics/election/2026/article/ken-paxton-john-cornyn-ad-spending-22210178.php" target="_blank" >outspent</a> Paxton and his allies by more than 3 to 1, Paxton <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/texas-senate-runoff-results" target="_blank" >trounced</a> Cornyn in their head-to-head match, winning by more than 27 points.</p><p>In addition to beating Paxton in the general election, Democrats <a class="Link" href="https://www.multistate.us/elections/results/texas-2026" target="_blank" >won</a> every other statewide contest in Texas, including the elections for governor, lieutenant governor and attorney general. That sweep was remarkable enough given recent Texas political history, and it was especially striking because Republicans <a class="Link" href="https://intel.crownatlasmedia.com/txbp/dashboard?year=2026" target="_blank" >outspent</a> Democrats by more than 5 to 1 overall and by <a class="Link" href="https://www.texastribune.org/2026/10/27/texas-governor-election-abbott-hinojosa-campaign-finance-fundraising/" target="_blank" >nearly 8 to 1</a> in the gubernatorial race, where Gina Hinojosa <a class="Link" href="https://apps.texastribune.org/features/2026/texas-general-election-live-results-2026/" target="_blank" >beat</a> the incumbent, Greg Abbott, by 7 points.</p><p>Beyond Texas, big spending likewise was no guarantee of victory. In the Ohio <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/11/03/amy-acton-beats-vivek-ramaswamy-in-ohio-governors-race/" target="_blank" >gubernatorial race</a>, Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy and his supporters <a class="Link" href="https://ohiocpa.com/news-resources/special-interest-sections-old/news/2026/10/30/week-in-review--nov.-1--2026" target="_blank" >outspent</a> Democratic nominee Amy Acton and her allies by nearly 3 to 1. Acton <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/ohio-governor-results/" target="_blank" >won</a> by 8 points.</p><p>Republican candidate Rick Jackson <a class="Link" href="https://www.ajc.com/politics/2026/10/rick-jackson-georgia-governor-race-spending/" target="_blank" >spent</a> more than $200 million of his own money on his <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/10/21/atlantas-former-mayor-is-running-for-georgia-governor-the-2020-protests-could-cost-her-the-race/" target="_blank" >campaign</a> for governor of Georgia. As of Oct. 20, <a class="Link" href="https://paidforpolitics.com/governors/ga" target="_blank" >spending</a> on Jackson's behalf totaled about $235 million, compared with $30 million for Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms. Despite that 8-to-1 financial advantage, Jackson <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/georgia-governor-results/" target="_blank" >lost</a> the race by more than 8 points.</p><p>Notwithstanding such <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2020/03/04/bloomberg-drops-out-demonstrating-the-limits-of-money-and-the-perils-of-arrogance/" target="_blank" >conspicuous</a> <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2019/12/30/billionaires-buying-elections-bloomberg-steyer-ad-blitzes-arent-moving-the-needle/" target="_blank" >counter examples</a>, a 2024 <a class="Link" href="https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/21582440241279659" target="_blank" >study</a> of House elections from 2000 to 2018 found that campaign spending was positively associated with victory. But as in <a class="Link" href="https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2008.00348.x" target="_blank" >earlier research</a>, the association was stronger for challengers than for incumbents.</p><p>In general, a 1% increase in campaign spending corresponded with a 6.5-point increase in the probability of winning. But for incumbents, the "marginal effect" was negative, especially when it came to contributions by special-interest groups.</p><p>The authors echoed the <a class="Link" href="https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11127-009-9425-z" target="_blank" >explanation</a> offered by <a class="Link" href="https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1017/S0022381611000934" target="_blank" >other researchers</a>: Although incumbents start with big advantages, including the name recognition, publicity, support networks and pork associated with their offices, they face "diminishing returns for the money spent on campaigning," such that "higher campaign spending does not help incumbents much to secure a seat." Challengers, by contrast, see "increasing marginal returns for each dollar spent" as they strive to overcome the benefits of incumbency.</p><p>Given that difference, limits on campaign spending are unlikely to reduce the dauntingly high <a class="Link" href="https://www.opensecrets.org/elections-hub/reelection-rates" target="_blank" >reelection rates</a> for members of Congress, which averaged about 93% for the House and 88% for the Senate from 2010 through 2024. To the contrary, such restrictions would further undermine competitiveness by making it even harder to throw the bums out.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-230000" name="module-230000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: No better reason for a feast than to express gratitude
entries.summary: <p>The feast we are about to enjoy is always a highlight of the year. The warmth of family and friends, the respite from work, the spirit of gratitude, but honestly, it's also about the food! A bit of a fanatic about staying trim, I watch every morsel of food I consume 364 days a year. But on Thanksgiving, <i>I feast.</i></p><p>If you think turkey is dry, you're not doing it the way my grandmother and mother taught me. Rub the bird all over (inside and out) with a generous amount of vegetable oil, tons of garlic, salt, pepper and paprika. Then roast it in a humble paper bag, such as you get at the supermarket. Ease the greasy, garlicky bird into the bag, being careful not to tear it, and then seal it with a stapler. It's the one day of the year when a stapler is a kitchen tool. </p><p>Some cooking sites recommend against this. Pshaw. Our family has been doing it this way for decades and we've never had anything but moist, delicious meat. The bag keeps moisture inside so that the breast meat doesn't dry out, yet it still emerges golden brown and shiny after its four or more hours in the oven.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4c0000" name="module-4c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>For the cranberry sauce, just do the relish recipe on the Ocean Spray bag. Throw the fresh berries into a food processor with a whole orange, including the rind, a half cup of sugar (or a little less) and a dash of cinnamon. Its tanginess perfectly offsets the heavy turkey.</p><p>I won't recite our whole menu, but I will report that it contains many more dishes, including sweet potatoes with a citrus glaze, lots of fresh vegetables, stuffing, Champagne and two desserts — one of which is a pumpkin flan with maple caramel from Ina Garten that is one of the best things I've ever tasted. How can you not smile?</p><p>There really is no better reason for a feast than to express gratitude. When George Washington proclaimed a day of Thanksgiving in 1789, he spoke of our thanks to God that we were able to form a government:</p><p>"That we may then all unite in rendering unto him our sincere and humble thanks — for his kind care and protection of the People of this country previous to their becoming a Nation — for the signal and manifold mercies, and the favorable interpositions of his providence, which we experienced in the course and conclusion of the late war — for the great degree of tranquility, union, and plenty, which we have since enjoyed — for the peaceable and rational manner in which we have been enabled to establish constitutions of government for our safety and happiness."</p><p>Presidents John Adams and James Madison also issued various Thanksgiving proclamations, but President Thomas Jefferson did not; he thought asking people to pray breached the separation of church and state (he was a stickler). But the November holiday wasn't firmly established until President Abraham Lincoln, who, relieved and grateful after the Battle of Gettysburg, decreed that the holiday would be celebrated henceforth on the fourth Thursday of November. The month before he delivered the Gettysburg Address, he wrote:</p><p>"I do therefore invite my fellow citizens in every part of the United States ... to set apart and observe the last Thursday of November next, as a day of Thanksgiving ... And I recommend to them that while offering up the ascriptions justly due to Him ... they do also, with humble penitence for our national perverseness and disobedience, commend to his tender care all those who have become widows, orphans, mourners or sufferers in the lamentable civil strife in which we are unavoidably engaged, and fervently implore the interposition of the Almighty Hand to heal the wounds of the nation and to restore it as soon as may be consistent with Divine purposes to the full enjoyment of peace, harmony, tranquility and Union."</p><h3>Focus on the positive </h3><p>If that sounds a bit prolix, don't blame our 16th president — it was apparently ghostwritten by Secretary of State William Seward, who originally thought he would have been a better president than Lincoln, but later became one of his most admiring and loyal subordinates.</p><p>In 1939, Franklin Roosevelt tried to move Thanksgiving to the third Thursday in November to elongate the holiday shopping season, but the new date was widely mocked as "Franksgiving" and the idea was scrapped by 1941.</p><p>It is not necessary to be religious to give thanks. Just focusing on the richness of our lives, on the many fortunate accidents that were necessary to bring us to this moment, on the bounty we have at our fingertips, on the support we enjoy from family and other loved ones, on the delight in ordinary pleasures like eating and drinking, on the fantastic genius of our ancestors who set this table for us with their political wisdom, their technical wizardry, their courage and their commitment to build a better future — all this we can recognize with full hearts.</p><p>Happy Thanksgiving!</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of the Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b40000" name="module-b40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Republicans: Go cold turkey on Trump
entries.summary: <p>With the dust finally settling after the 2026 midterm wipeout, we can look back and assess more clearly what just happened.</p><p>And while it’s clear that this election was a giant referendum on President Donald Trump and his party’s lack of focus and broken promises on affordability and the war, it’s also clear that corruption was a huge turnout driver as well.</p><p>A whopping 91% of voters across both parties, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/exit-polls" target="_blank" >exit polls</a>, said that government corruption was either crucial to their vote or a major factor, and it’s not hard to see why.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ed0000" name="module-ed0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Trump and his sons have grown richer by billions — with a “b” — since Trump returned to the White House, through defense contracts, crypto schemes and stock trades, an absolutely unprecedented amount of self-dealing.</p><p>Others in his orbit and administration are being accused of the same — of lining their own pockets, profiting off access to the president, insider trading on foreign policy and trade deals and more. The wheel of corruption never seems to stop spinning.</p><p>Democratic lawmakers will have a lot of material to work with when they take power in January, but what will Republicans do? For a decade they’ve protected and defended Trump’s many impolitic decisions, from lying about election results to instigating an insurrection at the Capitol.</p><p>But Trump, thankfully, is on his way out. And perhaps what we saw the most clearly through the midterms is how little he cares about the party he leads.</p><p>He did nothing to help Republicans win the midterms. He chose to primary safe Republicans and endorse terrible candidates like Ken Paxton in Texas, Mike Lindell in Minnesota, Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio and Darline Graham in South Carolina.</p><p>His war and tariffs boxed Republicans in on the economy, as did Trump’s messaging on affordability, which he routinely called a hoax.</p><p>He refused to let candidates run smart races, because he insisted voters pretend he was on the ballot. Everything he did, in fact, made it harder for Republicans to win.</p><p>He never cared about the party, but he especially doesn’t now that they’re effectively “losers.” He won’t do much to help put them in a better position for 2028. If the last three weeks are any indication, he’ll only continue to do things to imperil their chances.</p><p>So why would they help him?</p><p>Whether it’s allegations of crypto corruption, conflicts of interest on defense contracts, secretive slush funds or the burgeoning national security Nvidia scandal, Republicans should feel no loyalty to Trump whatsoever. Instead, they should do everything they can now to save themselves.</p><p>What does that look like? If I’m Secretary of State Marco Rubio, I’d resign yesterday. Anyone who has presidential ambitions should try to distance themselves from this administration and its terrible decisions immediately.</p><p>Republican senators, many of whom were just elected or reelected to six-year terms that will outlast Trump, should join with Democrats early and often in their investigations of corruption and incompetence, including against Trump Cabinet members, family members and Trump himself.</p><p>Republican House members, all of whom will be up in 2028, should demand an immediate end to the Iran war, an immediate and full release of the Epstein files and a rollback of Trump’s tariffs. They should publicly denounce Trump’s new chief of staff Stephen Miller when he inevitably does and says things that would only appeal to white nationalists. And House leadership should start recruiting candidates who don’t repel a majority of voters.</p><p>While it’s true that Trump has sufficiently doomed the Republican Party for cycles to come, lawmakers don’t have to totally go down with the ship. Their only salvation is cutting Trump loose now. And they don’t even have to feel bad about it. He’s already done it to them.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fa0000" name="module-fa0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Dear Abby: Adult feels judged for youthful outlook to all that's bad in the world
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> When major tragedies shake our world, my immediate instinct isn't to harden my heart or get cynical. Instead, I feel a profound need to protect my inner peace by holding on to a childlike state of mind. To me, retaining pure imagination, intense curiosity and joy in small things is a radical act of self-preservation. It's the emotional fuel that gives me the energy to keep going.</p><p>Unfortunately, many adults around me view this perspective as a lack of awareness or a refusal to grow up. They mistake my intentional wonder for immaturity. How can I effectively communicate to others that keeping my childlike innocence alive is not a flight from reality, but rather my shield against the darkness of the world? — <i>WONDERING IN THE WORLD</i></p><p><b>DEAR WONDERING:</b> For some, being an adult involves an acceptance that the world can be a dark and scary place. Your words alone are not going to convince those people that your state of mind is anything but Peter Pan syndrome. However, you can show them with your actions.</p><p>Even as you hold on to that youthful energy, always strive to be punctual, thoughtful and kind. Follow through on your promises and make wise decisions. If you consistently act like a responsible grown-up, your critics may begin to view your whimsy and exuberance as positive traits, not signs of true immaturity.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> When I asked "Janice" to marry me last spring, she was a pack-a-day smoker. I asked her to quit, and she promised she'd try. A few weeks before the wedding, she said she wouldn't be able to quit because of wedding stress. The week of our wedding, she was still puffing away, but I asked her to be smoke-free at least on our wedding day. Again, she said she would try.</p><p>Janice smoked heavily on our wedding day. She bummed a cigarette from a bridesmaid just a few minutes before the ceremony started. I could taste the tobacco when we kissed to seal our vows. Janice looked beautiful at the reception but smelled like an ashtray. There are even several pictures of her with a cigarette in her hand in our wedding album.</p><p>I haven't told my wife how disappointed I was that she smoked at our wedding. Should I? And why was she not able to put down her cigarettes for just that one day? — <i>DISAPPOINTED IN ALABAMA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DISAPPOINTED:</b> I see no reason for you to keep your feelings to yourself. While sharing them, however, please recognize that Janice appears to be severely addicted to tobacco. That's why she was unable to put her cigarettes down even for one special day.</p><p>Unless Janice is willing to enter a smoking cessation program of some kind, I seriously doubt she will ever be able to kick the habit. If children are to be a part of your future together, I recommend that she enroll in one before she becomes pregnant, because nicotine and tobacco smoke aren't healthy for babies or small children.</p><p>TO MY READERS: I hope Thanksgiving brings you and your families together in love and gratitude for our blessings. I'm thankful for each and every one of you and the wonderful conversations we've had over the years. Because I love hearing from you, and because I still see a number of letters being forwarded from the old Los Angeles address, I want to remind everyone of my new physical mailing address: Dear Abby, P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. — <i>LOVE, ABBY</i></p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i> </p>

entries.title: Giving Tuesday — a day when you're supposed to help the needy — is just around the corner
entries.summary: <p>Did you have a nice Thanksgiving? Eat a lot of turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, pumpkin pie?</p><p>Of course you did. Everybody does. But did you pause to wonder <i>why</i> you and everybody else ate all that? Probably not. Here, I'll tell you why: because you were supposed to. You might prefer steak. Or be on a diet. But someone who eats steak on Thanksgiving, well, is just strange. Ditto for anybody dieting. Not done.</p><p>Because Thanksgiving is a holiday. And human beings have a tendency to conform. The holidays come around, we do all sorts of things that are expected of us: travel across the country at great expense. Buy presents. Put on stupid sweaters. Gorge ourselves.</p><p>Dec. 1 is also a holiday: Giving Tuesday. If that doesn't sit at the forefront of your consciousness, perhaps it's because Giving Tuesday is only 14 years old, begun in 2012.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4a0000" name="module-4a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>But Giving Tuesday is a real holiday, and an important one, important for charities of all sorts and those they help. The day when ordinary people who are not in the habit of donating money to charities do so.</p><p>"Giving Tuesday is a soft-sell way to ask for support for those nonprofit organizations like ours who don't know how to or have time to ask for funding because we are too busy doing the work," said Fernando Jones, founder of Blues Kids Foundation, whose organization helps young people find their inner Buddy Guy or Koko Taylor. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/09/the-kids-feel-it-summer-camp-has-kids-singing-the-blues" target="_blank" >We met them</a> in July.</p><p>When that story ran, a well-known, wealthy Chicago woman was so moved she hurried over, heard their concert and gave Blues Kids a donation. (Which now you can too, at <a class="Link" href="https://www.blueskids.com/give" target="_blank" >www.blueskids.com/give</a>.)</p><p>Maybe blues aren't your thing. Not every charity is for every person, which is okay, because there are so many, you get to pick one that meshes with your interests. One of my favorite Chicago social service organizations is The Night Ministry, because the people they help need help more than anybody else. People who have nowhere to turn, who are living on a piece of cardboard in the street, depend on The Night Ministry, the last strand in our fraying social safety net.</p><p>"Homelessness continues to go up," said Carol Sharp, president and CEO of The Night Ministry. "There are over 68,000 people unhoused in Chicago. Of those, a little over 18,000 are young people. We offer access to stability and resources."</p><p>The Night Ministry sends a medical bus to poor areas of the city. It dispatches doctors with backpacks into places so cut off there isn't a road for a bus to roll upon — the lowest depths of Lower Wacker Drive, below the street that many are afraid to drive on. Now imagine living there.</p><p>"We serve more than 100,000 people who are experiencing homelessness," said Sharp, noting that this is The Night Ministry's 50th anniversary. "Sometimes we're the difference between someone surviving the night or not."</p><p>They need more than money. They need volunteers, especially medical professionals. Churches pick a spot and rendezvous with their medical bus and hand out sandwiches — my older son and I once did that. Making sandwiches is easy. They also hope to start offering places where indigent people can recuperate after surgery, and are looking for donated spaces to do that.</p><p>"Our mission has not changed," Sharp said. Well, maybe a little, in that they've gained a new supporter: you. You can contact them at <a class="Link" href="https://thenightministry.org/support/" target="_blank" >thenightministry.org</a>. Between Dec. 1 and Dec. 15, deep-pocket supporters are matching donations, dollar for dollar.</p><p>There are so many other causes, and you can match one to your concerns. Worried about surging antisemitism? Support The Ark, a charity that aids underprivileged Jews. Despite stereotypes, many Jews have trouble getting by.</p><p>"Population studies show that in 2020 one out of every five Jewish households is struggling," said Marna Goldwin, CEO of The Ark, which provides services, from delivering meals and running food pantries to offering dental care, mental health counseling and career guidance.</p><p>"The Ark is a place where you can see the impact of your dollars," said Goldwin. "See it really touching a person's life, the power of philanthropy." They can be reached at <a class="Link" href="https://arkchicago.org/" target="_blank" >arkchicago.org</a>.</p><p>I've seen all first hand — kids singing the blues, The Night Ministry's Crib shelter for LGBTQ+ youth, elderly people opening the door a crack to receive an Ark meal and their one human interaction for the day. Helping the organizations that help them feels great.</p><p>Come July 4, people across Chicago will be lighting off fireworks and frightening pets for one reason: because they're supposed to. Come Giving Tuesday, people all across the nation, perhaps including you for the first time, will turn to help others for the same reason.</p>

It is the city, not a particular person, that makes Morris football special.</p><p>This year’s squad has a strong offensive line, led by four-year starter Brogan Kjellesvik, and a solid overall team. Running back Mike Groesch has 17 TDs and 908 yards rushing. The Wildcats lost the final game of the regular season to rival Coal City, but have rolled through the playoffs and are a favorite to win their fifth state title on Friday.</p><p>Wilmington scored at least 35 points in every playoff game but allowed 20 points per game.</p><p>Running back Hunter Kaitschuck rushed for 1,467 yards and 22 TDs and Dane Van Duyne added 700 yards and 16 TDs for the Warriors this season. Quarterback Brysen Meents threw just 31 passes, but 10 were for touchdowns.</p><p>West Frankfort’s offense is more balanced, with quarterback Lucas Parker throwing for 1,630 yards and 21 touchdowns. Running back Chris Samples scored 23 TDs and rushed for 2,028 yards.</p><p>Keep an eye on Jase Bennett, who has nine interceptions this season for the Redbirds.</p><h3><b>Class 1A: Heyworth (13-0) vs. Brown County (13-0), 10 a.m. Friday</b></h3><p>Brown County returns to the 1A title game after losing to Lena-Winslow 58-13 last year. This is the first appearance in a state championship game for Heyworth. Neither team has won a title.</p><p>Running back/defensive back Braydon Laesch, lineman Jarrod Fulcher and and quarterback/defensive end Caleb Troha lead Heyworth while quarterback Michael Kassing paces Brown County.</p><p>“Laesch is our most electric playmaker,” Heyworth coach Scott Godfrey said. “He’s our leading receiver and rusher.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago's Thanksgiving parade draws hundreds to the Loop for a colorful burst of holiday spirit
entries.summary: <p>Under cloudy skies, this year’s Chicago Thanksgiving Parade kicked off an hour earlier, as planned, at around 7:45 a.m. from Ida B. Wells Drive and State Street. The procession, the event’s 92nd, moved along its route toward Randolph Street, featuring 14 balloon floats, 12 marching bands and interludes from numerous local cultural groups. This year’s parade introduced a new Cookie Monster balloon.</p><p>The earlier start was a programming accommodation to allow the parade's television broadcast to begin at 8 a.m. on CBS Chicago, ahead of the Chicago Bears' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/26/what-to-watch-for-in-bears-lions-game-ben-johnson-vs-amon-ra-st-brown" >Thanksgiving Day game</a> against the Detroit Lions.</p><p>Charles “Peanut” Tillman, a Bears cornerback for 12 seasons, was the parade's grand marshal. Actor Jake Connelly waved from a Mercedes convertible, just in front of the Nutcracker balloon float. The 14-year-old Arlington Heights native played Derek Turnbow in the final season of Netflix's “Stranger Things.” Tillman and Connelly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/10/13/chicago-bears-edition-of-hallmarks-holiday-touchdown-is-a-gooey-homage-to-the-city" ><u>make appearances</u></a> in “Holiday Touchdown: A entries.title: Bulls executive VP Bryson Graham has a lot to be thankful for lately
entries.summary: <p>There are almost 72 million reasons the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> front office was thankful on Thursday.</p><p>It starts with a 5-3 record over the last eight games first and foremost, showing signs of life after a dismal 1-9 start thanks to a brutal schedule to begin the regular season.</p><p>But front offices are big-picture focused and having almost a projected $72 million in cap space heading into the 2027-28 season was the flexibility that executive vice president of basketball operations Bryson Graham was diligent in wanting to create.</p><p>Between the current standings and the books, two very important bricks in the foundation that could accelerate the Bulls rebuild.</p><p>Making sure to have roster flexibility doesn’t need much of an explanation. Graham knew that veterans Isaac Okoro and Jalen Smith were on expiring deals, while Norman Powell, Zach Collins and Tre Jones are signed through the 2027-28 campaign but as team options.</p><p>That means the Feb. 11 NBA trade deadline might be a really fun time for Graham and his staff.</p><p>There was a second part to this Year 1 for Graham, however. Because of the new 3-2-1 draft lottery system, the VP wanted to be fluid with contracts but good enough in the standings to finish in the sweet spot of bottom four through 10.</p><p>The non-play-in teams that reside there will have the best chance at No. 1 in the draft at about 8.1% each. The bottom three teams — which the Bulls looked like one of a few weeks back — have just a 5.4% chance at the top selection.</p><p>And while this 2027 class doesn’t even belong in the same conversation as the 2025 Cooper Flagg class and then the current ’26 batch of rookies, it’s starting to build out at the top and in backcourt positions that the Bulls might be coveting.</p><p>Current starting point guard Josh Giddey was extended by the former front office so there is no allegiance to the veteran by his new bosses, while Powell’s shooting guard spot could be vacant come the deadline.</p><p>So who are the names that should be on Graham’s radar? It’s a list that might be five deep:</p><p></p><h3>1. Quentin Coleman, Illinois </h3><h3></h3><p>The one player carrying all the buzz heading into December is the Illini guard who has shown a solid shooting touch from three-point range (36.4%), but also an uncanny athleticism at the rim despite his wiry frame.</p><p>What has caught the attention of the scouts, however, is his do-everything ability, leading his team in rebounds (6.8 per game), assists (4.7) and steals (2.8). While Andrej Stojakovic’s 46 at Duke a few weeks ago captured the headlines, Coleman put in 27 points, grabbed eight rebounds and handed out four assists with three steals.</p><p></p><h3>2. Caleb Holt, Arizona </h3><h3></h3><p>The athletic freshman projects out as a two guard, but at 6-foot-5 and a solid 215 pounds, has wing written all over him. His 24-point, nine-rebound performance against Auburn was an eye-opener, and the fact that he’s also shooting just under 40% from three-point range carries weight.</p><p></p><h3>3. Jordan Smith Jr., Arkansas </h3><h3></h3><p>Forward Tyran Stokes was the preseason No. 1 player in the class and has changed nothing about that. Smith was in that No. 2/No. 3 range and has faded a bit. He’s listed as 6-2 and that might be a question, and his scoring has been inconsistent.</p><p></p><h3>4. Stefan Joksimovic, International</h3><h3></h3><p>A 6-7 point guard from overseas, anyone? Buyer beware. His jumper has been sketchy so far this season and there are concerns his defense could be an issue. The positional size and creativity in his passing and scoring, however, have scouts drooling.</p><p></p><h3>5. Alijah Arenas, USC </h3><h3></h3><p>Want scoring? Think Gilbert Arenas’ son, Alijah. Knee surgery derailed his freshman campaign, but the scoring guard has been more than making up for it.</p>

entries.title: How Blackhawks' special-teams success has propelled ongoing surge
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> coach Jeff Blashill likes to reference this stat: when NHL teams outscore their opponents on special teams, they win something "like 76% of games" on average.</p><p>For the Hawks this season, the power play specifically has been a remarkable harbinger of success. They're 9-1-2 when they score at least one power-play goal and a ridiculous 0-13-0 when they don't.</p><p>So it's no surprise that, during their current 5-1-1 surge, they tout the hottest power play in the league. </p><p>They're 11-for-20 during these seven games, boosting them from last in the NHL at 9.8% on Nov. 8 all the way up to 14th at 22.5% now.</p><p>Patrick Kane's return to health and Sam Rinzel's breakout have been key. With lefty Kane on the right flank and right-handed Rinzel at the point, they're well-positioned to set each other up for one-timers. Rinzel has also gotten better at getting his one-timers through on goal, generating more rebounds.</p><p>Frank Nazar's shooting accuracy from mid-range has improved, as well, and rookie Roman Kantserov continues to prove effective in the bumper role in the slot.</p><p>It's amazing that the power play's success has (so far) continued without Connor Bedard, too. Tyler Bertuzzi was promoted back onto the top unit following Bedard's injury, and Bertuzzi's "human backboard" approach — forming a wall at the back post for bank-in goals — has been made more useful by the rest of the unit's fast puck movement.</p><p>That fast movement was especially noticeable <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/22/blackhawks-canucks-roman-kantserov-hat-trick" >Sunday</a>, the Hawks' first game with three power-play goals since Jan. 7. Their confidence and chemistry was palpable, and the Canucks' penalty kill was forced to keep changing shapes until they eventually broke down.</p><p>Once the Hawks created isolated two-on-one or three-on-two advantages down low, Bertuzzi, Kantserov and Nazar's collective eagerness to crash the net really shined.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">The puck movement by the Blackhawks’ PP was fantastic leading up to this goal in Vancouver: <a href="https://t.co/cKyRk3sVgS">pic.twitter.com/cKyRk3sVgS</a></p>— Ben Pope’s Video Clips (@BenPopeCSTclips) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCSTclips/status/2126027711332175933?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 26, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>"We've broken [in] well, we've won battles [and] we've done a lot of good process things," Blashill said. "Sometimes the power play clicks and the process isn’t great. I think the process has been good."</p><p>The analytics agree. Per Natural Stat Trick, the Hawks' power play ranked 32nd in scoring chances per minute (0.39) through Oct. 12, then 13th in chances per minute (1.07) from Oct. 13 through Nov. 8, and now fifth in chances per minute (1.14) since then.</p><p>Meanwhile, the penalty kill has been less of a bellwether of overall success this season, but it, too, has ticked up lately. </p><p>The Hawks have killed 23 of their opponents' 27 power plays over their last eight games, elevating their "PK" from 15th in the NHL at 78.2% to 11th at 80.5% now.</p><p>"We're in the middle of the pack," Alex Vlasic said Sunday afternoon. "That's what it feels like: we're doing some good things, but then we'll let in a goal every other game. I think we're heading in the right direction."</p><p>Vlasic's intuition was correct. The Hawks went nine-for-nine on the kill against the Canucks and Kraken, marking just the second time they've recorded consecutive unblemished games this season. To their credit, though, they've allowed more than one power-play goal against only once all season.</p><p>Per Natural Stat Trick, the Hawks' penalty kill ranks 15th since Nov. 6 in scoring chances allowed per minute (0.94), compared to 23rd before that (1.11). They've also allowed the fifth-fewest shot attempts per minute since Nov. 6.</p><p>They haven't yet rekindled last season's great success — they finished second in the NHL at 83.6% — but Ilya Mikheyev was a major contributor to that.</p><p>The fact they're still above-average without Mikheyev is a good sign that Blashill's unique killing system isn't too personnel-dependent. Cole Smith, Anton Frondell and Nazar have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/11/blackhawks-penalty-kill-anton-frondell-frank-nazar-roles" >stepped in</a> and done well, as has Teuvo Teravainen.</p>

entries.title: Bears TE Colston Loveland carted off with knee injury
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — Tight end Colston Loveland was carted from the injury tent to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>' locker room in the first quarter Thursday. He suffered a knee injury and was quickly ruled out for the game, an ominous sign for his availability in the weeks to come. </p><p>Loveland appeared to have been hurt after being shoved backward by linebacker Trevor Nowaske and over running back D'Andre Swift at the end of a two-yard run. </p><p>Loveland sat on the back of the golf cart with a white towel over his face as he was driven to the tunnel.</p><p>Earlier in the first quarter, Loveland fumbled the ball away after being hit following a five-yard catch and run. He was hit by Lions safety Brian Branch and cornerback DJ Reed. </p><p>He entered the game with 40 catches on 60 targets for 392 yards and three touchdowns. He's spent half the season without fellow tight end Cole Kmet, who was lost for the season had knee surgery after a grisly injury against the Patriots. </p><p>Rookie Sam Roush is the Bears' third tight end, followed by veteran Stephen Carlson. Injuries to the Bears' tight ends present a challenge for coach Ben Johnson, who is traditionally among the league leaders in using offensive sets with multiple tight ends.</p>

entries.title: How will the MLB lockout affect the White Sox and their offseason?
entries.summary: <p>At 10:59 p.m. on Dec. 1, MLB offseason activity will stop. Images of active <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> players will disappear off the team website, their social media accounts will stop posting hype videos. It will be weird.</p><p>MLB owners are expected to lock out the players’ union (MLBPA) when the current collective bargaining agreement expires, under the guise of expediting negotiations for a new one. It helps that most of the baseball world experienced this process five years ago, but everyone knows this is happening. Even Sox manager Will Venable, as careful of a communicator as there is, discusses this as nearly fait accompli.</p><p>“Knowing that there's a lockout potentially coming, we’re making sure that we're all dialed in and have everything aligned with our players, and that the guys are really supported to go out and have a productive offseason,” Venable said last week. “There's a lot of work that's been coming with that.”</p><p>Venable was alluding to rules barring team employees from contacting MLBPA members (players on the Sox 40-man roster) while the lockout persists. Theoretically, larger, league-altering changes could result. As an increasingly public-facing push from the league’s social media arms have indicated, owners want a salary cap. Their most recent proposal involved setting a salary <i>floor</i> of roughly $180 million; a figure the Sox have only met twice (2022, 2023) in history and would need to add over $50 million to Cots’ Contracts estimate of their current payroll to meet.</p><p>But that most recent league proposal would give teams until 2028 to get into compliance, and the MLBPA has maintained — for decades — that a salary cap is a non-starter. Amid an impasse unlikely to resolve until both sides feel the pressure of potentially canceled games, the White Sox and most teams are proceeding with business as usual. For example, the league has proposed an International Draft, but the Sox still anticipate bringing in strong 2028 and 2029 IFA classes under the present system. Life goes on, until we hear otherwise.</p><p>With all those unknowables, the one thing the White Sox can prepare for is to be out of contact with their players. Venable said Sox coaches have expedited their offseason check-ins with the roster in anticipation. But as they prepare for offseason training goals like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/18/grant-taylor-excited-to-join-white-sox-rotation-that-should-see-another-addition-this-winter" target="_blank" >Grant Taylor stretching out as a starter</a>, Sox players plan to keep tabs on one another.</p><p>“There's a great group of guys already that were with us last year that have already texted me,” said Taylor. “I was with Sean Burke [last week] just talking through some different things on how excited we were to be able to work together.”</p><p>All the inside joke t-shirts and elaborate coordinated celebrations last season were nice, but this winter is where the White Sox’ much-lauded team chemistry will really get put to use.</p><p>“This team was special for a reason,” said third baseman Miguel Vargas. “I got a couple of teammates, they come in [for] some vacation and fly to Miami, they stay at my house and we are about to go practice together.”</p><p>At this point, the roster’s connectivity is largely taking the form of group text threads and regular FaceTime calls with each other, but Sox players told the Sun-Times that similar gatherings to train and practice together are expected to come together, especially as the lockout — expectedly — stretches into January. Nashville, where Burke, Colson Montgomery, Caleb Bonemer and others live in the offseason, is one potential gathering point.</p><p>“What our group was able to do last year was work out together, communicate well, and that was really led and driven by the players,” Venable said. “That was them on their own, and they're still going to be able to go in and do that.”</p><p>So while efforts to improve the Sox roster still dominate the news cycle, the team hitting 2027 spring training in stride — whenever it begins — will rely on the same traits that made them better than the sum of their parts in 2026.</p><p>“Our clubhouse, our group,” general manager Chris Getz said. “That was our superpower.”</p>

entries.title: Man slain over weekend in Gage Park shooting identified
entries.summary: <p>A 20-year-old man who was fatally shot over the weekend in the Gage Park neighborhood has been identified. </p><p>Kevin Garcia Martinez, 20, was sitting inside his vehicle in the 2700 block of West 51st Street about 12:45 a.m. Saturday when two assailants fired guns at him, Chicago police and the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>An autopsy Sunday determined Martinez, of Gage Park, died of multiple gunshot wounds and his death was ruled a homicide, according to the medical examiner's office. </p><p>The attackers sped away in a blue car south on Washtenaw Avenue and have not been arrested, police said. </p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Isaiah White prevails in close race in Downtown and Near North Side District 6a Chicago School Board
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/6a/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 6a</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: Near North Side, West Town</i></p><p>The candidate supported by a billionaire-backed political group and charter proponents won over two progressives, according to final official results from the Chicago Board of Election Commissioners released this week.</p><p>With all precincts reporting, 103 votes separated Isaiah White, a school support worker, from Anusha Thotakura, the appointed incumbent who runs a statewide advocacy organization. Brenda Lee Anderson, a Northwestern University lecturer on leave, trailed White by 1,072 votes.</p><p>In a statement, Thotakura's campaign said they were filing a petition for a recount. </p><p>"Every vote matters, and in a race this close, a careful second look is the responsible step," her campaign said in the statement. "This is a routine, lawful part of the election process, and we are following it as written."</p><p>The campaign added that they would accept the final outcome. </p><p>As ballots have been added to White's total in the weeks since Election Day he has consistently remained in the lead. </p><p>The close race was somewhat unexpected. Voters in the area typically support more conservative candidates. But across the city, candidates like Thotakura, who were supported by the Chicago Teachers Union, did better than expected after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/11/06/chicago-school-board-ctu-teachers-union-spending" >being significantly outspent</a>. </p><p>CTU-endorsed candidates won <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/11/18/in-cps-win-jessica-biggs-took-precincts-across-the-city-but-her-coattails-were-not-long-data-shows" >10 of 20 board seats</a>. If the recount changes the outcome of the race in District 6a, which is rare, that total would become 11, giving CTU-supported members the majority of the board seats. Board president-elect Jessica Biggs, who completes the board at 21 and sets the board meeting agendas, won election with the backing of anti-CTU supporters.</p><p>In addition to support from the CTU, Thotakura was also endorsed by the Service Employees International Union, which represents school support workers. She seems to be splitting the more left-leaning vote with Anderson, who was not backed by any special interests.</p><p>More than $500,000 was spent on White’s campaign by The Urban Center, a centrist political organization that advocates for school choice across public and private schools, and the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools. He also was endorsed by an anti-CTU political action committee that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”</p><p>Given its location as part of the commercial and business center of the city, District 6a has just 14 public schools — the fewest of any school board electoral districts — and none are neighborhood high schools. The students who attend Chicago Public Schools here <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F#districtNumber=6a" target="_blank" ><u>include a more diverse mix than in most districts</u></a>, but the schools have more white and Asian American students than CPS as a whole.</p><p>Two of the schools in the district have the highest rating given by the state; while 60% had the lowest two distinctions, “developing” and “comprehensive,” according to 2026 state data. There are now six levels of designations, up from the five up last year when the bottom two were called “comprehensive” and “intensive.”</p><p>Thotakura’s and White’s main priorities are to boost reading and math scores. Anderson’s main goal is to fix CPS’ chronic budget crisis.</p><p><i>Contributing: Reema Amin, Chalkbeat Chicago and Kate Grossman</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ab0000" name="module-ab0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Chicago School Board election results</b><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-99ebbb22-d88c-11f1-a0f8-2966deb425a8"><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-results" target="_blank" >What you need to know about all 21 races</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/11/06/chicago-school-board-ctu-teachers-union-spending" target="_blank" >Political groups spent $12 million to defeat CTU candidates. One losing race cost $76 per vote.</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-teachers-union-poised-to-capture-half-of-school-board-district-seats-but-likely-to-lose-presidency" target="_blank" >CTU poised to capture half of school board district seats, but loses president’s race</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-president-results" target="_blank" >Jessica Biggs wins president race</a></li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Marching Illini will march on at postponed Thanksgiving Day parade, fundraising for $175,000 in extra costs
entries.summary: <p>The Marching Illini has opted to keep on with their performance at the rescheduled Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Saturday, citing potential costs for students.</p><p>The decision was made Thursday evening in a <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1B5ANsU3Ce/" target="_blank" ><u>video</u></a> posted to social media featuring band director Barry Houser. An hour earlier, the band had posted a <a class="Link" href="https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.givecampus.com%2Fcampaigns%2F49878%2Fdonations%2Fnew%3Futm_id%3D97758_v0_s00_e0_tv4%26fbclid%3DIwZXh0bgNhZW0CMTAAcGRvZgVicmlkETFRWEFuQXNpYVVWYkhxQkJyc3J0YwZhcHBfaWQQMjIyMDM5MTc4ODIwMDg5MgABH5Ov5WqR9wn6oPAC_sUA48XafwtnJkSqRGQAoH2KsiDjfayrGZjvlyRyRRcN_aem_JYCKvW01HMzXSAUa6XD8YQ&h=AUDqTlKyCDkRmEdvA4IesmEJtVxvEPRWYXS2x72GTW6VOBmR6koYMK4r0RA8Oku9jOGH-BFgRlSWaGIZcGEbN4jIKwZix7Nvu685D7hjlcKA0y1k9knEnBlEAFwz71PkuU_VLGuCpTlA1XsEBlT17dXpgEIuicFtKMNRHw&__tn__=-UK*F&c[0]=AUADlhpP14boT6wHpC753ozhVFx9C5PJwYXWhY7joJzSHfxBvKGrXVmP-ejO5To8MfV-MlJSf-ZYcXhhIDO_aYMEo5T5B9AVqfvH_muJgj5A91VpOCTjt6eRJfaVnEnR-svKCrLWetUKKRjaun0cHd1McsRYD3ZgGst9DdlD7n-h3vRMgvqStDD_yEVhBxMOqhP9qTmXMEtfpU-Xs2yZdMmG_w" target="_blank" ><u>fundraiser</u></a> asking the university community to donate to help ease the extra lodging and transportation costs, which they estimated would total an additional $175,000 to the $600,000 the trip had already incurred.</p><p>The parade was rescheduled after concerns over the safety of participants and spectators due to expected “extreme weather.”</p><p>“My friends, we are doing this parade on Saturday,” Houser said to cheers and applause from students.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="FacebookUrl"> <script>(function(d, s, id) { var js, fjs = d.getElementsByTagName(s)[0]; if (d.getElementById(id)) return; js = d.createElement(s); js.id = id; js.src = "//connect.facebook.net/en_US/sdk.js#xfbml=1&version=v20.0"; fjs.parentNode.insertBefore(js, fjs); }(document, 'script', 'facebook-jssdk'));</script><div class="fb-post" data-href="https://www.facebook.com/reel/1887337082437614"></div> </div> </div> </div></div><p>In total, the originally planned $600,000 trip came with a cost of $275 for each student, while the rest of the trip was covered by donations and grants, according to the band. The band had boarded buses to New York City Sunday after performing at the final Illini home football game of the year Saturday.</p><p>“We are grateful that our students have the opportunity to represent the University of Illinois in this historic parade but its postponement and extending our stay in New York City presents significant challenges,” Houser said in a statement on social media.</p><p>The group, made up of 410 members, is one of 10 marching bands that had been selected for this year’s rendition of the century-old, annual holiday tradition. It would have been its second time performing in the parade, the first coming in 2015.</p><p>Wednesday night, the band set up in Times Square to perform after videos of their rehearsal of Sufjan Steven's song "Chicago" went viral online.</p><p>In a statement to the Sun-Times, Houser said the band was “working through logistics of student schedules, bus and hotel availability, and finally expenses associated with this extended stay.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="FacebookUrl"> <script>(function(d, s, id) { var js, fjs = d.getElementsByTagName(s)[0]; if (d.getElementById(id)) return; js = d.createElement(s); js.id = id; js.src = "//connect.facebook.net/en_US/sdk.js#xfbml=1&version=v20.0"; fjs.parentNode.insertBefore(js, fjs); }(document, 'script', 'facebook-jssdk'));</script><div class="fb-post" data-href="https://www.facebook.com/photo/?fbid=1703088361188853&set=a.204220617742309"></div> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Parade organizers had not offered assistance to the bands, Houser said. A representative for the parade’s organizers didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Organizers announced the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/11/25/macys-thanksgiving-day-parade-postponed-saturday-bad-weather" target="_blank" ><u>parade’s postponement</u></a> Wednesday afternoon.</p><p>In a statement, NBC cited conversations with the city and concerns over the safety of participants and spectators due to expected “extreme weather.” A rerun of the 2025 parade aired Thursday and the parade was pushed to 8:30 a.m. Saturday, Macy’s said in a statement.</p><p>A representative for the Marching Illini confirmed to the Sun-Times Wednesday that the band had also been informed of the postponement by Macy’s and NBC.</p>
